transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Lina Morales (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (CTO - Oceanic AI), Maya Singh (ML Eng), Ravi Patel (Infra)

[00:00] Jamie: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll do a quick intros and then dive into your cost questions around hosted vs dedicated, um Lina's gonna cover the profiling side.
[00:12] Ethan: hey thanks Jamie, appreciate it. I'll kick off with context - we run a customer-facing doc summarization API, about 150k monthly active users, peak concurrency around 800 real-time requests. Latency target is sub-400ms 95th for short docs. Budget-wise we have something like $10k-$15k monthly initially for infra, curious where that maps to per-token.
[00:33] Lina: cool, thanks Ethan. quick clarifying q - average document length in tokens?
[00:38] Maya: so average request ends up being ~350 tokens in, 120 tokens out. but distribution is heavy tail - some long runs to 2k tokens occasionally.
[00:48] Jamie: got it, so typical round-trip ~470 tokens. for hosted, we price per-token with a base rate and tiered discounts as you scale - Lina can show how batching and prefix caching change effective unit cost.
[01:05] Lina: yeah i can. one caveat, the transcription might say "KV cash" sometimes, it's KV cache - so caching often cuts your cost a lot if requests share prefixes or session context.
[01:18] Ravi: can you give a ballpark? like for 470 tokens how much on hosted?
[01:23] Jamie: ballpark, for a standard 13B model on hosted, list price would be around $0.004 per 1k input tokens and $0.02 per 1k output tokens — that maps to roughly $0.000002 per input token and $0.00002 per output token, so per-response maybe around $0.001 roughly. but importantly batching and caching can reduce that.
[01:46] Maya: wait that math seems off, can we run that slower?
[01:49] Jamie: yeah sorry, to be clearer: if you do 470 tokens total and you pay say $0.02 per 1k tokens (output) and $0.004 per 1k input, the raw call cost is small fractions of a cent. but the big driver is volume and latency SLOs leading you to dedicated pools which change economics.
[02:08] Ethan: when does dedicated start being better?
[02:11] Lina: generally when you have predictable sustained throughput and need lower unit cost and isolation. with Dedicated you reserve GPU capacity, we give you committed throughput and lower per-token internal billing — plus you can tune batching aggressively. A rule of thumb: if you exceed a sustained equivalent of ~100M tokens/month or need consistent sub-200ms p95, dedicated often pays off.
[02:33] Ravi: 100M tokens seems high — our projection at scale could hit 40-60M tokens. how does caching factor? we have a lot of repeated prompts due to templates.
[02:42] Lina: caching helps a lot. prefix/KV cache can reduce effective token compute by serving cached KV states for repeated prefixes. In practice customers with template-driven requests saw 20-60% reduction in per-token compute. so 60M effective tokens could look like 25-40M compute tokens after cache depending on overlap.
[03:01] Maya: is that automatic or do we modify code?
[03:04] Lina: Redwood does automatic prefix detection and optional cache layers, but some engineering to key requests and session affinity helps. for hosted there's managed cache, for dedicated/private you can tune cache sizes per pod.
[03:17] Ethan: what about batching? we care about latency — can batching help without hurting 95p?
[03:22] Lina: batching trades latency for throughput. continuous batching with latency caps can keep 95p within SLO for many workloads by forming small batches under e.g., 10-30ms queuing. If you're at high concurrency, batching reduces GPU idle time and lowers per-token cost substantially.
[03:39] Jamie: and a thing folks miss — combining caching and batching often yields multiplicative gains: fewer tokens to compute and larger batches for the remaining tokens.
[03:48] Ethan: curious about pilot economics — if we run a 30-day pilot expecting 10M tokens during that time, what do we pay hosted vs dedicated?
[03:58] Jamie: quick back of envelope: hosted for 10M tokens at $0.02 per 1k ~= $200. With input tokens cheaper maybe add $40, so $240 single-model. But that's pure token charge; net costs may include rate-limits and not guarantee latency. Dedicated would have a minimum monthly commit — typically starts at a few tens of thousands per month depending on GPU class. For a 30-day pilot, dedicated probably not worth it unless you need latency SLAs.
[04:24] Ravi: what about burst capacity? we can't provision for peak but need to handle traffic spikes.
[04:29] Lina: Dedicated has burst pools and autoscaling policies. Redwood can route overflow to hosted at higher unit cost, so you get predictability on base load and safety valve on spikes.
[04:38] Maya: does Redwood support quantized models to lower cost? we care about output quality for summarization though.
[04:44] Lina: yes, quantization and model variants are part of Optimize. we recommend A/Bing quantized variant against FP models — often 8-bit or 4-bit gives 1.5-3x throughput depending on model with small quality deltas for summarization tasks. We'll share past evals.
[04:59] Ethan: ok can you share real customer numbers? we want to show to finance.
[05:04] Jamie: i can share anonymized TCOs — e.g., a mid-market SaaS with ~50M tokens/month moved from hosted to dedicated and saw 30-45% reduction in token spend after caching and quantization, but they had a monthly committed spend of $25k.
[05:20] Ethan: in that case might be borderline. our budget isn't $25k to start.
[05:24] Jamie: understood — that's why pilots often start hosted, we instrument to measure effective compute tokens after cache and batching, then use that telemetry to model Dedicated savings.
[05:34] Maya: what's the instrumentation look like? we need token-level cost breakdowns and latency per route.
[05:38] Lina: Redwood Console shows token breakdown by route, model and user, plus tracing hooks. We can expose exporter metrics for your observability stack.
[05:47] Ravi: security — if we used Dedicated or Private, what about KMS and audit logs?
[05:53] Jamie: Dedicated includes infra isolation; Private gives full VPC/on-prem option with customer-managed KMS/HSM, SOC2, full audit logs and longer retention as an add-on. We'll include compliance docs.
[06:05] Ethan: any hidden costs — egress, data retention?
[06:09] Lina: egress depends on region and is typically pass-through. Data retention and extended observability has add-on pricing. We'll call those out in the spreadsheet.
[06:18] Maya: i want to dig into the batching numbers — can you show example throughput on a T4 vs H100 for our request profile?
[06:25] Lina: quick rules of thumb: H100 gives much higher throughput and lower latency for large models; T4/RTX have higher p99 and lower throughput. For small models and quantized paths T4 can be cost-effective. For your 470-token avg and concurrency 800 spikes, H100 or A100-class may be needed for sub-400ms p95 with no aggressive batching. We'll prepare model/hardware mapping in the benchmark doc.
[06:50] Ethan: do you offer a calculator where we plug our traffic and it estimates cost and hardware?
[06:54] Jamie: yes, we'll send a TCO calculator spreadsheet — that's part of the pricing packet.
[06:58] Ravi: about integration — do pilots require much infra changes? we run k8s on GCP with strict egress controls.
[07:05] Lina: hosted has a simple API and SDKs — minimal infra change. Dedicated can be run on your VPC with peering; Private is the most involved. We'll document network requirements.
[07:15] Ethan: timeline — we want to pilot in Q1. is that feasible?
[07:19] Jamie: absolutely, timeline sounds fine. Pilot steps: instrument traffic, run 2-week benchmark with sample logs, then 30-day pilot hosted w/ telemetry. If metrics justify, move to Dedicated planning.
[07:31] Maya: what's the SLA for hosted?
[07:33] Jamie: hosted has best-effort, but we provide response SLOs in the contract for enterprise customers. Dedicated includes stronger latency SLOs and uptime guarantees.
[07:44] Ethan: competitors — we're also talking with Anthropic and evaluating an internal self-host. how do you compare on raw unit price?
[07:51] Jamie: prices vary; Anthropic tends to be a bit higher for safety-tuned models, OpenAI competitive. The key is operational cost — staffing to run self-host adds ops cost. Our pitch is predictable serving and lower ops overhead plus tooling to reduce unit compute beyond raw price.
[08:06] Ravi: Ops cost number would help — can you provide a model for headcount + infra vs Redwood managed?
[08:12] Jamie: yes will include a simple headcount-op model in the TCO.
[08:17] Maya: what's sample data we'd need to run your benchmark?
[08:20] Lina: sample logs showing request times, tokens in/out, concurrency patterns, and a few representative prompts. We'll give a checklist.
[08:27] Ethan: okay that sounds good.
[08:29] [longer section of Q&A where Jamie and Lina answer detailed followups about warmup, seq length optimizations, and KV eviction policies, with occasional transcription errors]
[18:45] Lina: ...and just to call out, for KV eviction we use LRU-ish policies and you can tune per deployment, though the transcribed notes sometimes say "LRU, you know, or LUV" which is a transcribe quirk.
[19:03] Maya: (laughs) okay noted.
[19:10] Ethan: any gotchas around billing reconciliation? we want per-team cost centers.
[19:15] Jamie: Redwood Console supports per-route cost tagging and exported billing reports. You can break down by user/team/model.
[19:23] Ravi: curious about fallback routing — if Dedicated is overloaded will Redwood auto-route to hosted? what's the cost and config?
[19:30] Lina: yes you configure overflow policies; overflow to hosted is charged at hosted rates and is visible in the Console. We'll show an example policy.
[19:39] Ethan: final question on privacy — we need to ensure no PII persists.
[19:44] Jamie: we support data redaction hooks and configurable retention. Private gives you full control on retention and audit logs.
[19:51] Maya: good.
[19:53] Jamie: ok i want to recap next steps — we'll send pricing spreadsheet & TCO, benchmark checklist, and schedule a technical deep dive next week; action items for both sides as noted.
[20:05] Ethan: sounds good, thanks all.
[20:07] Jamie: thanks, we'll follow up via email.

[47:00] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings, named entities like H100 sometimes transcribed as H-one-hundred, KV cache as KV cash. natural speech patterns present.
